The no-code app

Source: vignettes/the-no-code-app.Rmd
the-no-code-app.Rmd

pilotr ships a point-and-click application over the same design specification that the R and Python packages consume. It is a thin client. Every control writes into the portable JSON specification, which you can download and run unchanged in either package to obtain identical data.

Two ways to run it

One way is to run it on your own machine. With the package installed, launch the app locally:

pilotr::run_app()

Each user runs their own R process, so a power run never holds up anyone else. Within the app, each power analysis or power curve runs in one R process, and the app waits for its result. With the future and promises packages installed, run_app() runs it in a background process, leaving the app free for other sessions, such as a second browser tab. For a heavy run, download the specification and call power_design() or power_mixed() from the console, whose workers argument spreads the replicates over your local cores.

The other way needs nothing installed. A serverless build runs entirely in the browser through WebAssembly, with no server and nothing uploaded. Try it at the no-code app. It covers the light path: build a design, simulate, inspect the data, estimate two-group Gaussian power with the sample size its curve solves to, and export.

What the app does

Describe the design in the left panel: the sample sizes, the factor and its two levels, the fixed intercept and effect, a response family, and for crossed designs the random-effect standard deviations. A within design crossed with items can use counterbalanced lists, which show each subject each item in one condition and rotate the conditions over subjects and items, and its specification then declares version 0.4. Then read the tabs. Both apps open on ‘Guide’, which describes the controls, the response families and the analyses. Three of the other tabs have shorter names in the browser build, given here in brackets after the installed app’s. ‘Design spec (JSON)’ (‘Design spec’) holds the exact JSON specification, the portable source of truth, and ‘Data’ the simulated data set. ‘Summary & plot’ gives group summaries and a plot. ‘Power & design analysis’ (‘Power’) reports simulation-based two-group Gaussian power with the Type S and Type M errors, together with a power curve over sample size and the sample size at which that curve reaches 0.80, with a confidence interval on it. The curve adds sample sizes until it brackets a power of 0.80, and for a design without random effects or continuous predictors the tab also gives the sample size power.t.test() computes, as a check. The tab runs this analysis for a two-group Gaussian design with one row per subject, and for any other design it explains how to run it in the installed package. ‘Reproducible R script’ (‘R script’) emits a self-contained, reproducible R script, which ends by suggesting the analysis that fits the design. In the installed app, Verify runs that script in a clean R session and checks that its data are identical, bit for bit, to the data the current specification produces. The comparison is with the specification in force when you select Verify, so it does not depend on when you last selected Simulate.

Changing the response family resets the intercept and effect to sensible values for that family’s scale, so a point-and-click design stays valid. The advanced ‘paste a JSON spec’ box accepts designs beyond the point-and-click controls, such as continuous predictors, interactions and nesting.

‘Data’, ‘Summary & plot’ and the data download show the last simulation, and the ‘Data’ tab and the name of the downloaded file give the seed it used. The specification, power and script tabs and the specification download follow the controls as they stand. When the controls change the design after a simulation, a note above the tabs says so until you select Simulate again.

One specification, three interfaces

The app does not own the design. The specification does. Download the specification (.json) or the data (.csv), and run the specification unchanged in R with simulate_design() or in Python with pilotr.simulate() for the same data, identical to the last bit wherever R and Python share a maths library (see the cross-language article). The app rounds Gaussian and reaction-time responses to four decimals and leaves a Beta response unrounded, for the reason ?build_spec gives. The heavier analyses stay with the installed packages: crossed mixed-effects power in R, through lme4 as the reference backend, and in Python, through statsmodels, and precision/ROPE design analysis in R. Whichever interface you use, the specification you build in the app drives all three.
